title: When Difficult Math Feels Easy: Atomising Multi-Digit Subtraction with Regrouping
author: Samantha Lippert
summary: Samantha Lippert, a third-grade teacher, applies atomisation to multi-digit subtraction with regrouping and shows how the "curse of the expert" hides the prerequisite skills a novice needs. Working backward from the learning outcome of solving a three-digit problem such as 567-178, she identifies three atoms: whether numbers are ready to subtract (categorical and factual atoms taught with Boulton's non-example/example sequence), unbundling numbers into "funny numbers" (a transformation atom taught with number bonds, independent of subtraction), and the standard algorithm as a routine atom with sub-atoms for tens, hundreds, both, and zeros. Each atom comes with a scripted teacher and student exchange using mini whiteboards and choral response. She is explicit about what she will not teach, namely the "More on the floor" mnemonic and a menu of competing strategies, because they can substitute for understanding why regrouping preserves value. The result is a worked model of how to turn a standard into a teachable sequence.
points: The curse of the expert makes teachers collapse several prerequisite skills into one "simple" procedure, so the first job is to identify the steps explicitly.
Subtraction with regrouping decomposes into categorical, factual, transformation and routine atoms, each taught and checked before they are coordinated.
Teaching "funny numbers" (renaming 23 as 1 ten and 13 ones) separately from the algorithm makes subtraction across zeros far less error-prone.
The author deliberately omits the "More on the floor" mnemonic and multiple parallel strategies, arguing mnemonics should not replace the underlying place-value reasoning.
Scripted question sequences with whole-class mini-whiteboard responses give continuous checks for understanding and make misconceptions easy to spot.
quotes: The curse of the expert describes what happens when our own expertise makes it difficult to recognize the steps a novice needs to take to reach the same level of understanding. We see the finished skill. We forget the learning that made it possible.

Before we can teach a complex concept, we have to break it down into its component parts, or atoms. We then teach those atoms explicitly and systematically, building from what students already know toward the skill we ultimately want them to master.
This is why we often see kids who subtract up when solving multi-digit subtraction, when they should be regrouping in order to solve the problem.
The traditional way we would teach this is to “borrow” from the tens, teaching the student to cross out the 3 in the tens place, make it a 2, and then give 10 to our ones place making it 11.
Students are learning to rename a number across multiple place-value units before they encounter the subtraction algorithm.

A mnemonic is not inherently incompatible with conceptual understanding. The problem arises when a mnemonic replaces the teaching of the underlying mathematics or becomes the student’s only means of deciding what to do.
Ultimately, atomisation isn’t about slowing math down just to make it easy. It’s about breaking complex skills into teachable pieces so that every student has access to the underlying mathematics.
